title: How To Use Music To Make Routines More Fun And Effective un-and-effective/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin shares a strategy learned from colleague Rick Morris for using music to cue and pace classroom routines. Instead of verbal signals, a teacher plays a piece of music sized to the length of the routine, which both launches the activity and acts as a built-in timer that moves students along before the song ends. He suggests starting small, such as pairing a 60-second song with lining up to leave the room, and recommends Televisiontunes.com as a source of recognizable, appropriately timed TV theme songs. The piece frames the strategy as a way to inject energy and cooperative spirit into transitions that might otherwise feel like drudgery.
points: Music can replace verbal cues to launch routines, while its length also functions as a built-in timer pacing the activity.
Choosing music that matches a routine's ideal length requires some planning and practice with the class beforehand.
Recognizable, well-paced songs (e.g., TV theme songs) increase energy and cooperation during otherwise mundane transitions.
Televisiontunes.com is recommended as a free source of short, familiar songs suited to classroom routines.
Starting with a simple routine and a short song (about 60 seconds) is the recommended way to introduce the strategy.
quotes: Routines are the lifeblood of a well-run classroom. But it’s important they’re viewed in a positive light.
A forceful or militaristic approach leads to boredom and dissatisfaction. The constant starting and stopping, the stern reminders, the hard stares and impatient body language
Many years ago, my friend Rick Morris of New Management shared with me a simple way to cultivate this spirit through music.
What’s so cool about this strategy is that the music both cues the start of the routine and sees to its conclusion.
A great resource is Televisiontunes.com, where you can find thousands of free songs from every television show imaginable.
